title: Dear An AUsome Life: the family plan is too much
summary: An editorial example about proposing a smaller gathering clearly, without turning private support needs into a family debate.
search: Home/The library/A good questionA good question · Advice · 3 minute readDear An AUsome Life: the family plan is too muchAn editorial example about proposing a smaller gathering clearly, without turning private support needs into a family debate.By An AUsome Life · Editorial guidePrint this guideIn this guideDecide what works before explaining itKeep the first message shortShare practical information privatelyMake the smaller plan realAnswer pressure without adding a new argumentLeave room for the next invitationThis is an editorially constructed question, not a submitted reader letter. The question: “Our relatives have planned a long holiday day with several stops. We would like to see them, but the whole schedule does not work for our household. How do I suggest something smaller without making it sound as though we do not want to come?” Begin with the part you can genuinely offer. A clear, smaller plan gives people something to respond to. You can be warm about seeing relatives and definite about the amount of the day your household can manage. Decide what works before explaining it Look at the actual journey, activity and support available. Include the time before and after the gathering, not only the hour printed on the invitation. Ask the people affected what they want, using their usual communication and support. A plan should reflect their preferences as well as the practical limits. Choose one workable option. It might be lunch at the first stop, a visit on another day or meeting relatives for a short activity closer to home. Avoid offering three alternatives you cannot really manage in the hope that one will sound agreeable. Keep the first message short A constructed example: “We would love to see everyone. We can join you for lunch from one to two, then we will head home. The later stops will be too much for our day, so please go ahead without us.” Change the wording and times to suit the relationship and the actual decision. The message names the connection, the commitment and the limit. It does not ask the recipient to diagnose your family situation or decide whether your reasons are sufficient. Share practical information privately If a specific arrangement would make the visit possible, ask for it. You might need to confirm the entrance, the meal time or a place to sit. Explain the practical point to the person who can help, rather than giving a group chat a detailed account of somebody else's needs. Privacy is particularly important when the explanation concerns a child or another person who has not agreed to public discussion. You can say that a schedule does not work without proving it through intimate information. Make the smaller plan real If you agree to lunch, arrange the transport and departure so that lunch can actually remain the plan. Avoid relying on someone who expects to stay for the whole day unless a separate return is confirmed. Tell the host whether you are bringing food or need anything held aside. If a person wishes to pause or leave earlier, keep that possibility in view. A shorter plan should not become another fixed obligation that ignores the people it was meant to help. Answer pressure without adding a new argument A relative may suggest that you stay and see how it goes. If you have already decided, repeat the useful information: “Lunch is what works for us this time. We are looking forward to it.” You do not need a longer explanation each time the same question returns. If new information genuinely changes the options, consider it. Being clear does not mean refusing to hear a practical suggestion. The decision still belongs with the people whose day and support are affected. Leave room for the next invitation Afterward, thank the host for the part you enjoyed or the arrangement that helped, without promising a larger visit next time. A successful small gathering can become a familiar option, but one good day does not obligate anybody to repeat the same schedule indefinitely. Our family-life guides place dignity, preference and ordinary enjoyment at the center. summary: A small working agreement can prevent crossed wires, surprise bills, and confusion about who speaks for the family.

Which documents should you send? Who emails school? What if the advocate takes a position you do not share? A short planning conversation at the beginning can make the relationship more useful and much less mysterious. The plan can fit on a page. It does not replace a service contract or legal advice about one. It records the practical details that are easy to assume and important to say aloud. Give the work a first destination Describe the concern in everyday language, then choose a first deliverable. For example: “We need help understanding the progress reports. Please review the current IEP and these two reports, then give us a short list of questions for the next meeting.” This illustrative scope is easier to evaluate than “fix everything.” It gives the advocate room to identify missing information while giving you a clear point at which to review the work and cost. Ask what they can reasonably assess from the records, what requires discussion with the Team, and what is outside their expertise. A good working plan can include uncertainty. It should not depend on promising a particular school, service, or outcome. Agree on five practical details The initial task. List the documents to review and the question to address. Include what the advocate will produce: a preparation call, written questions, meeting attendance, or another clearly described item.The budget. Record the agreed scope, billing terms, and when additional work requires your approval. Clarify charges for short messages and conversations.Communication. Choose a contact method and reasonable response expectations. Identify what should happen if the matter becomes urgent or the advocate is unavailable.Authority. State whether the advocate may contact school, whom they may contact, and which messages you want to review before sending. Define any permission to share records narrowly enough to understand.Review point. Set a date or milestone to decide whether the arrangement is helping and what, if anything, comes next. Before uploading records, ask how files are stored, who can access them, how long they are retained, and how you can obtain or remove your copies when the work ends. Avoid sending a complete personal history when a smaller, relevant document set will answer the current question. Plan the meeting roles Federal IDEA permits parents to invite other individuals with knowledge or special expertise regarding the student, and the inviting party determines that knowledge or expertise. Team membership and the expertise provision. Tell the school who is joining and their role as a practical preparation step. Discuss roles with the advocate first: will you open the meeting, will they take notes, and when should they ask questions? Agree on a simple way to request a private pause if you need to confer. You might say: “I will introduce our priorities. Please help us clarify the data and note any unanswered questions. If you think a new issue needs to be raised, check with me before changing our approach.” Adapt this example to the support you actually want. Make room for the student's perspective Explain how the student communicates interest, discomfort, agreement, or refusal, and identify who can help interpret observations responsibly. Distinguish what the student has expressed from what adults infer. The advocate should help keep those distinctions visible, particularly when the student does not use speech. A meeting about a teenager should use language and materials that respect their age, even when they require substantial assistance. Sensitive personal-care details should be discussed only with the people who need them for the educational question. Review the partnership after the first task Ask yourself: Do I understand the recommendations? Were the agreed limits respected? Can I raise a concern without feeling rushed or dismissed? Did the work give us a clearer next step? The FCSN advocate guide describes helping parents become stronger advocates as an important part of the role. Support should leave you better informed about the choices ahead. If the arrangement needs adjustment, name the adjustment directly before the next billable task begins. title: Five, fifteen or thirty minutes to a more usable home.
summary: A room-by-room reset for the time and energy actually available. Start with the walking route, make one space useful and stop at a clear finish line.

Choose a finish line you can reach. A household reset is a short pass that makes the next part of the day easier. Pick five, fifteen or thirty minutes. Decide what “done” means before moving anything: a clear route through the house, a usable kitchen counter, or somewhere comfortable to sit. The plans build on each other. The fifteen-minute plan includes the first five minutes; the thirty-minute plan includes the first fifteen. If care, work or life interrupts, stop at the end of the current small action. Gather: one rubbish bag, one basket for misplaced objects, a laundry basket, two clean cloths, a suitable surface cleaner and a timer. Keep bathroom and kitchen cloths separate. First, make one decisionToday's useful finish line: [clear walking route / usable food-prep space / ready-to-use bathroom]. Time available: [5 / 15 / 30 minutes]. Anything else is optional. The five-minute rescue. This is the version for an unexpectedly busy afternoon. Stay in the rooms you actually need next. Minute 0–1, route: clear the path from the entrance to the kitchen, bathroom and usual seat. Move shoes against the wall, put bags on their hook and remove trip hazards. Keep exits and mobility routes clear.Minute 1–2, kitchen: take cups and plates to the sink or dishwasher. Scrape scraps into the bin. Put food away promptly; if safety is uncertain, follow appropriate food-storage guidance rather than the reset timer.Minute 2–3, rubbish: collect obvious rubbish from the counter and seating area. Leave ambiguous papers alone. Tie the bag if full and put it in the usual disposal place.Minute 3–4, one surface: clear a tray-size working patch. Return things with nearby homes; put the rest in the temporary basket. Wipe the patch with a product appropriate for the surface.Minute 4–5, landing place: clear one seat and the space beside it. Return the phone, remote or communication device to its familiar accessible position. Put cleaning supplies away. Stop here: the route is open, dishes are contained and one surface is useful. A closed bedroom door can wait. The fifteen-minute everyday reset. Complete the rescue above, then add these three small jobs. If another adult is helping, give them one room and a finish line rather than “help tidy.” Minutes 5–9, kitchen: load dishwasher-safe items or wash the few dishes needed for the next meal. Clear the sink enough to use it. Wipe the main preparation area, then the table. Leave a soaking pan contained, with its handle safely out of the way. Minutes 9–12, bathroom: put personal items back in their usual places. Check toilet paper, hand soap and a clean hand towel. Wipe visible splashes from the basin and tap with the bathroom cloth. Pick clothing up from the floor. This is a quick readiness check, not a substitute for cleaning a soiled toilet.Minutes 12–15, living area: put loose laundry into its basket. Fold one blanket. Return up to five objects from the temporary basket to homes you already know. Place the basket out of the walking route and name a later time to finish it. Stop here: the kitchen can handle food, the bathroom has its essentials and the main seat is free. Skip styling cushions, matching towels and sorting charging cables unless one of those is today's actual problem. The thirty-minute room-to-breathe version. Use the extra fifteen minutes for a short floor pass and tomorrow's bottleneck. Minutes 15–20, floors: sweep or vacuum the kitchen crumbs and the main walking route. Spot-clean a spill with a floor-safe product and dry the area. Leave moving furniture and cleaning under beds for another day.Minutes 20–25, bedroom or laundry: choose one. Put dirty clothes in the hamper and straighten the bed; or fold and put away one small basket of clean laundry. Start a wash only if someone can move and dry it later. Minutes 25–28, entrance: pair the shoes needed tomorrow. Put the correct bag in its usual place, with any already-agreed essentials. Keep keys secure in their established location. Do not rearrange a familiar system without discussing it.Minutes 28–30, finish: empty the temporary basket as far as time permits. Put any remaining items in one named spot with a specific return time. Store products, hang cloths to dry and wash your hands. Stop here: tomorrow begins with one fewer search. If something repeatedly lands in the same wrong place, consider moving its home closer to where it is used. Try that change before buying another organizer. Make the routine easier to live with. For a quieter reset, use a silent timer and do the sweeping while the room is empty. Say which space will change and for how long. Keep a familiar seat available. Ask before moving sensory items, an arranged collection or communication equipment. Offer one concrete optional action: “Would you like to put these three towels in the basket?” A demonstration, picture or two-item choice may be more useful than a running commentary. Match support to the person and respect a no. Older teens deserve age-appropriate materials and decisions, whatever help they need. Keep upkeep small: two minutes after the evening meal for dishes and rubbish; five minutes once a week to empty the temporary basket. If the basket never empties, reduce what goes into it or give those items a permanent nearby home. Cleaning safety: follow labels and never mix cleaning products. Keep chemicals away from children and pets, ventilate as directed and allow the stated wet contact time if disinfecting. Ordinary cleaning is often enough; illness or particular health risks may call for more. See the CDC's home cleaning and disinfecting guidance. A checklist to print or tick here. Keep the packet's cooking directions.1 jar, approximately 24 ounces / 680 grams, tomato pasta sauce: choose a flavor your household already enjoys.2 cans, approximately 15 ounces / 425 grams each, cooked white beans: cannellini or navy beans, drained and rinsed before serving.1 tablespoon olive oil: optional, for the finished dish.½ teaspoon dried oregano: optional; leave it out if the sauce is already well seasoned.½ cup pitted olives: optional, served separately with their own spoon.4 sealed fruit cups, approximately 4 ounces / 113 grams each: or one approximately 20-ounce / 567-gram can of fruit, divided four ways.Water and salt: use the pasta packet's water guidance; salt is optional and can be adjusted at the table. For two, use half the pasta and sauce, one bean can and two fruit cups. Refrigerate opened ingredients according to their labels. For six, multiply by one and a half: 18 ounces pasta, 36 ounces sauce, three bean cans and six fruit cups. Use a pot big enough for the larger quantity. Store this group in one ordinary box or beside each other on a shelf. Keep a manual can opener nearby. Put a note on the box: “Four-person pasta meal. Replace anything borrowed.” No special storage bins required. A twenty-five-minute assembly plan. Minutes 0–3: check and set up. Confirm the guest's food needs, read labels and wash hands. Fill the pasta pot as directed on its packet and bring it to a boil. Set out four bowls and a colander. Clean can lids before opening.Minutes 3–7: build the sauce. Drain and rinse the beans. Put the tomato sauce, beans and optional oregano in the saucepan. Heat gently, stirring so the bottom does not catch. Add 2–4 tablespoons water if it is very thick. Follow any heating instructions on the sauce and bean labels.Minutes 7–18: cook the pasta. Once the water boils, add the pasta and set a timer for its package cooking time. Stir. Keep the sauce at a gentle simmer while the pasta cooks, stirring occasionally. Put olives in a separate dish and set out the fruit.Minutes 18–22: check and combine. Test pasta for the texture wanted. Before draining, carefully reserve ½ cup cooking water. Drain. Combine with the sauce, or keep them separate if preferred. Add reserved water a tablespoon at a time if the sauce needs loosening.Minutes 22–25: serve. Divide into four bowls. Add olive oil if using, then offer toppings separately. If the pasta needs longer, follow its directions; there is no prize for meeting the timer. For someone who prefers unmixed foods, reserve their plain pasta before combining. Keep a familiar backup available if the person wants it. They do not need to try a new sauce to join the meal. Useful substitutions, without a second shopping trip. No white beans: use two same-size cans of chickpeas. The texture will be firmer. Keep them separate if that suits the group.No jarred sauce: combine one 28-ounce / 794-gram can of crushed tomatoes, 1 tablespoon olive oil and ½ teaspoon dried oregano. Simmer gently for 10–15 minutes while the pasta cooks; season to taste. It will be less rich than many prepared sauces.No pasta: use four portions of shelf-stable, ready-to-heat rice prepared exactly as its packet directs. Spoon the bean sauce over it. Do not assume a particular pouch is ready to eat cold.Gluten-free requirement: choose appropriately labeled pasta and check the sauce and toppings. Use clean equipment and discuss cross-contact needs with the guest.More people than food: cook extra pasta and open extra beans in the same proportions. A can of vegetables served separately can add another side; four portions do not become six just by changing bowls. Ten-minute, no-hob alternative for four: only if the products are labeled ready to eat, drain and rinse the two cans of beans, then toss with 2 tablespoons olive oil and 1 tablespoon vinegar. Offer approximately 8 ounces / 225 grams of crackers, the olives and fruit alongside. This is a lighter meal. Check ingredients and each person's usual texture requirements. Keep the shortcut food-safe. “Shelf-stable” applies to suitable unopened products. Anything labeled “Keep Refrigerated” belongs in the fridge, including some canned foods. Check the USDA's explanation of shelf-stable food. Do not use leaking, bulging or badly dented cans, or jars with compromised lids. Do not taste suspect food to check it. The USDA's canned-food guidance explains warning signs and storage. Serve promptly. If holding food, keep hot food at 140°F / 60°C or above and cold food at 40°F / 4°C or below. Refrigerate perishables within two hours, or one hour above 90°F / 32°C. Discard food that exceeds those limits. Divide leftovers into shallow containers for prompt chilling. These are the FDA's buffet-safety rules. Allergies need a direct conversation, original labels and suitable preparation. Keeping toppings separate does not by itself prevent cross-contact. See FDA food-allergy guidance. The five-minute restock. Replace pasta, sauce and both bean cansReplace four fruit portionsCheck oil, optional toppings and the can openerMove older suitable stock to the frontKeep labels and cooking directions with the food Copy checklistReset checksAfter guests leave, write down what actually needed replacing. Keep the kit to foods your household will also eat on an ordinary Tuesday.

title: Communication is an ecosystem, not a device.
summary: A practical, evidence-informed field guide to multimodal communication: speech, gestures, signs, gaze, objects, photos, AAC, typing, scanning, low-tech backups, communication partners, and using what is already around you.
search: The Communication Field Guide · Updated October 2026 Communication is an ecosystem, not a device. A word. A look toward the door. A familiar gesture. The actual cereal box. A photograph on a phone. A symbol. A typed sentence. A speech-generating device. A switch. A sound. More than one of these, in the same hour. Multimodal communication means keeping enough reliable routes open that a person can say what they mean in the place, body, energy level, and moment they are actually in. Make a communication cardUse what is around you → Evidence and links checked October 3, 2026. This is practical family guidance, not an individualized AAC evaluation. Field note no. 01The best route is the one that works now.The polished answer is not always the useful one. Sometimes the right communication tool is sophisticated technology. Sometimes it is the photograph you took in the parking lot thirty seconds ago. Prestige is not the point. Being understood is. In this guideThe whole toolboxUse what is around youPartner skillPrimary + backupReal-life settingsAI as drafting helpCommunication belongs to the personSources 01 / The whole toolbox There is no prize for using only one route. Augmentative and alternative communication is broader than a particular app or device. ASHA describes AAC as multimodal: people may combine speech or vocalizations, gestures, signs, facial expression, body movement, objects, photographs, visual supports, writing, text, symbols, communication boards or books, speech-generating technology, and different access methods. The mix can change with context, audience, purpose, motor access, fatigue, and sensory conditions. A good system therefore asks two questions at once: What does this person have to say? and what is the easiest reliable route for saying it right now? AaSpeech + vocalizationWords, approximations, sounds, laughter, intonation, and other intentional vocal signals. ✋Gesture + signPointing, reaching, conventional gestures, manual signs, and familiar movements. ◉Gaze + bodyEye gaze, facial expression, orientation, movement, and established body signals that can be confirmed. ●Real objectsThe actual cup, shoe, snack, ticket, towel, or item in front of you can make a choice concrete immediately. ▧Photos + visual scenesCamera-roll pictures, venue photos, screenshots, visual schedules, maps, and pictures of real choices. ✎Drawing + writingSketching, handwriting, note apps, typing, texting, saved phrases, and text-to-speech. ▦Symbols + low-tech AACSymbol displays, communication books, printed backups, and small situation-specific boards alongside robust language. ▣Speech-generating technologyDedicated devices, tablets, and phones with robust symbol- or text-based communication systems. ↳Switch + scanning accessDirect or indirect access that lets a communicator select from available choices using an established signal. The field ruleDo not make speech the tollbooth.Speech is one route. It should not be the price of admission to choice, attention, participation, humor, refusal, privacy, or an ordinary conversation. More than requesting A full communication life includes asking, refusing, commenting, complaining, joking, greeting, telling news, correcting someone, asking questions, changing the subject, seeking help, saying “not that,” and ending the conversation. A system that can only produce “I want” is carrying far too little of the person’s life. Behavior can tell you that something changed. It cannot safely tell you the whole sentence. Pacing, movement, vocalization, withdrawal, reaching, or a facial change may tell a familiar person that something is different. Treat that as information worth responding to, not as permission to assign a precise meaning. “Something seems different—can we figure it out?” plus an accessible way to answer protects agency better than deciding what the person meant. 02 / The useful art of improvising Use what is already around you. Communication does not stop because the perfect material is in another room. Real objects, signs, menus, packaging, maps, tickets, photos, screenshots, timers, calendars, a notes app, a dry-erase board, and the environment itself can all make a message easier to understand or express. These are additions and backups—not reasons to take away a person’s established AAC. At a caféUse the actual menu.Point to categories. Show the picture of the soup. Compare two real items. Let a person point, type, use their device, gesture, or say “none of these.” Keep food choice, size, drink, and “finished” as separate decisions. At the grocery storeThe shelf is already a visual display.Hold up two packages. Point to the cart. Use a saved photo of the familiar brand. Photograph a new item so it can be talked about later. The real object often carries more information than an abstract placeholder. On an outingPhotograph the next step.Take a picture of the entrance, the ticket booth, the pool door, the car, or the bench where a break can happen. A phone camera can turn an unfamiliar sequence into a concrete one in under a minute. At homeLet the house do some of the talking.Use the actual cereal box, bath towel, shoes, calendar, timer, laundry basket, or remote. Pair words and AAC with objects already attached to the routine. In a medical officeMake the invisible visible.A body diagram, mirror, photo, typed note, or showing the relevant body area can reduce language load. Prepare words such as stop, break, hurts, not sure, explain again, and where. Online or in a groupUse the side doors.Chat, advance questions, a shared document, typed responses, and a follow-up message can make participation possible when real-time turn-taking is too fast. A communication tool already in the room still counts. The aim is not to create a Pinterest-perfect support system. The aim is to make meaning easier to send and receive without taking control away from the communicator. The camera roll is a surprisingly good communication drawer. Photos can set a topic, show a person or place, represent a choice, clarify which item someone means, prepare for a visit, or help recall what happened. Use current, meaningful pictures where possible. A photograph of the actual pool is often more useful than a generic blue square labeled “swim.” Visual supports can explain what language alone leaves fuzzy. A short sequence can show where we are going, what happens first, what happens next, where a break can happen, and how we get home. Keep the sequence flexible enough for real life. If something changes, show the change rather than pretending the original plan is still true. 03 / The person across the table matters too The communication partner is part of the system. Research on AAC partner instruction repeatedly points to partner behavior as consequential. The device can be charged, the vocabulary can be excellent, and communication can still collapse if the people nearby rush, quiz, answer for the communicator, or only notice conventional speech. Speak to the person.Ask the communicator the question. A supporter can help with access or context without becoming the person being addressed. Wait longer than feels natural.Looking, motor planning, navigating vocabulary, composing, or switching routes takes time. Silence is not an emergency. Model, do not quiz.Use the communication system while you talk when appropriate. Demonstrate language without turning every interaction into a test. Make “no” work.Offer choices that can genuinely be refused. Include stop, break, finished, not sure, and something else. Respond to credible attempts.A word, look, gesture, device selection, typed message, or established signal deserves a response even when the answer to the request is no. Repair honestly.“I think I missed that. Can we try another way?” is better than pretending to understand. Do not move communication out of reach.Ask before touching or relocating a personal communication device. Communication access should not be treated as a reward. Check the environment.Noise, glare, seating, positioning, battery, volume, Wi-Fi, visual clutter, and fatigue can all make a familiar route much harder. Field note no. 02Partner skill can lower the effort of being understood.Good support does not make the message for the person. It makes room, time, access, and another route when the first one is difficult. 04 / Redundancy is civilized Choose a primary route and a backup before you need the backup. Electronics lose power. Sunlight makes screens hard to see. Pools are wet. Restaurants are loud. Motor access can change with fatigue. A familiar staff member is absent. Planning two workable routes ahead of time keeps an ordinary problem from becoming a communication emergency. YESNOSTOPBREAKHELPFINISHEDNOT SURESOMETHING ELSE Before leaving the house The person’s primary communication tools are charged, mounted, packed, or otherwise available. A low-tech or lower-effort backup covers the urgent messages that matter in this setting. At least one adult knows the person’s reliable yes/no or selection signals. Situation-specific words have been added without taking away access to the rest of the person’s language. There is a plan for water, glare, noise, a dead battery, a broken mount, or a device that suddenly refuses to cooperate. The person can refuse, change course, and end the activity—not only request it. Turn this into a field card ASHA guidance supports ongoing access to AAC and multiple modalities; concerns about ordinary recreational “screen time” do not apply to a screen being used for communication. 05 / Ordinary places, different demands Build the route around the setting. PoolKeep the device dry. Keep communication wet-proof.A waterproof or laminated backup can cover stop, more, out, bathroom, cold, help, finished, and something else. Establish how yes/no will work in the water. Keep the full system nearby in a safe dry place. RestaurantA menu is both language and clutter.Use the actual menu, photos, pointing, text, or a short display. Separate the decisions: entrée, side, cup or glass, more, finished. Keep “none of these” available. School or programConsistency is not sameness.Keep core language and access available across rooms and people. A brief communication profile, charging plan, backup, and access notes make the system less dependent on one familiar adult. Medical visitThe historian should not replace the patient.Ask the person first when possible. A supporter can clarify history and access while still leaving room for the patient’s own yes/no, stop, pain, fear, not sure, and questions. High stressLower effort, not expectations of personhood.Stress may make a usual communication route harder. Offer a familiar lower-effort route, reduce competing sensory demands, wait, and keep urgent messages easy to reach. New peoplePut the interaction rules on one small card.“Please speak directly to me. I communicate using [routes]. Give me about [time] to answer. If that route is hard, try [backup]. Please do not [ ].” 06 / AI can do the clerical work Let AI format the support. Do not let it invent the person. AI can be genuinely useful for turning known facts into a clean card, simplifying a venue’s information, organizing a visual sequence, formatting current choices, creating a plain-language version, or drafting a handoff. The safe dividing line is authorship: the tool may help organize and present information; it should not claim to know what the person thinks, wants, understands, or feels. Good useTurn real facts into a visual plan.Give the AI the actual location, sequence, photos or descriptions, break option, and way home. Ask for a short plan using only those facts. Good useMake current choices easier to scan.Paste today’s actual menu or activity choices. Ask the AI to group them clearly without adding unavailable options. Good useProduce two reading levels.Keep the meaning the same while asking for a compact card and a fuller staff note. The details stay consistent; the presentation changes. Good useTranslate a known message.Translation can help bridge languages. Preserve the original alongside the translation when precision matters and verify important wording. Do notAsk AI to read someone’s mind.Do not turn a photo, behavior, movement, or supporter’s hunch into a claimed statement of what the person wants or feels. Do notUpload private history because the prompt has an empty box.Use the minimum information needed for the communication task. A restaurant host does not need a medical chart to wait fifteen seconds for an answer. Free shared toolThe Communication Card MakerEnter the routes, yes/no signals, wait time, backup, and practical notes. It creates a printable field card, a one-page profile, and a reusable AI prompt.Open the generator → 07 / Agency first Communication belongs to the person. Support can make access easier without taking over the message. The aim is not for a partner to become a better guesser. The aim is for the communicator to have reliable ways to initiate, choose, refuse, clarify, disagree, repair, and end an interaction. Final selections stay with the communicator.Suggestions, prediction, modeling, or visual organization can reduce effort. The person still chooses the message. Interpretation is labeled as interpretation.If a supporter thinks a behavior may mean discomfort, say “I wonder if…” and seek confirmation rather than presenting the guess as the person’s statement. Unexpected answers are allowed.A communication system should make it possible to disagree with the supporter, pick the option nobody predicted, or introduce a new topic. Repair is shared work.When meaning is unclear, both people can slow down, change route, add context, and try again. Field note no. 03Presume a right to communicate, not a message you have already decided.Respect means access, time, useful language, and the freedom to surprise the person who thought they knew the answer. 08 / Sources + further reading Where this field guide is grounded. ASHA Practice Portal: Augmentative and Alternative CommunicationClinical overview of multimodal AAC, no-prerequisite access, selection techniques, partner training, intervention, and ongoing adaptation. CommunicationFIRST: Communicating in Times of StressPractical guidance on changing communication access under stress, using multiple routes, and preparing a short information page. CommunicationFIRST: Best Practices for Online Meetings with AAC UsersAdvance questions, adequate response time, chat and asynchronous participation, and avoiding interruption while someone composes a message. AssistiveWare: Planning for communication when AAC is not availablePractical multimodal backups using gestures, photos, real objects, writing, environmental clues, and low-tech supports. Kent-Walsh et al.: Communication partner instruction meta-analysisResearch synthesis on partner-instruction strategies for people who use AAC. Smart Predict (Augmentative and Alternative Communication, 2025)Research on partner-suggested vocabulary and conversational efficiency; useful as an example of technology supporting selection rather than replacing it. Individualized assistive and communication technology review (2026)A current look at emerging access technologies and the importance of individualized usability. The evidence base and technology change. The practical principles here are deliberately separated from individualized clinical recommendations. For a person-specific AAC assessment, involve appropriately qualified professionals and the communicator themselves. Take the useful part with youMake a card. Print it. Copy it. Use it with AI.The free generator turns the details that matter into something another person can actually use in the next ten minutes.Make a communication card →

title: One good plan. Room to enjoy it.
summary: The pretty part is easy to find. These are the details that help a family day out or a weekend away actually work: beds, food, water, waiting, and somewhere to pause.
search: Field notes · New England weekendsOne good plan. Room to enjoy it.The pretty part is easy to find. These are the details that help a family day out or a weekend away actually work: beds, food, water, waiting, and somewhere to pause.From our family notebook · New England weekendsThe weekends we remember best are usually the ones we did not overfill.We went north with the usual collection of things that makes a family weekend possible: more chargers than people, swim things, familiar food, one bag that had somehow become the bag for everything, and a plan that looked considerably shorter than the plans we used to make. That last part turned out to be the important one.Maine did not need much help from us. We had a room in Wells where the indoor pool could be the event instead of the reward after a day of sightseeing. We could unpack enough to know where the important things were, swim, come back, eat something easy and decide what—if anything—we wanted to do next. A hotel is much more useful to us when it behaves like a small home base than when it behaves like a glamorous place we are afraid to muss up.Freeport worked the same way. Once we stopped treating the whole town as a shopping assignment, L.L.Bean became its own outing: the giant boot, the fish, a wander through things made for weather, one or two things actually worth looking for, and then out. Kennebunk gave us ice cream that felt like an event without taking over the afternoon. Kittery gave us the very glamorous combination of affordable food in a bag and a gorgeous old fort by the water, which may be one of the most efficient ways to feel as though you have properly gone to Maine.None of these moments was enormous. That is the point. We have become collectors of small, repeatable family pleasures: the pool you can go back to twice, the bookstore where everybody can wander at a different speed, the coastal view you can enjoy without first walking three miles, the familiar meal that prevents the beautiful part of the day from collapsing under hunger.So this section of An AUsome Life is not really about “doing New England.” It is about finding the version of New England that still feels good when everybody is actually there. title: Their interests. Their choices. The help they need.
summary: An older teen can need substantial support and still want a say in clothes, activities and everyday life. Begin with the person, then make the practical details work around them.

Start with a real interest. Swimming, music, food, a favorite film, being outside: an activity has a better starting point when there is something the person enjoys in it. Ask in the way they communicate, allow time, and pay attention to their response. Familiar preferences can help you offer possibilities without deciding everything for them. Keep the choices real. If there is time for either a short walk or a visit to the pool, offer those. A long list of unavailable activities makes the decision harder for everyone. Show the actual item or place when that is useful.Break a large choice into smaller ones: activity first, then time or what to bring.Include a way to say “no,” “something else,” “break” or “finished.”Use the person's established communication methods and usual support. Age-respectful does not mean policing someone's taste. A much-loved character, toy or familiar activity can remain a genuine favorite. Present choices respectfully and let the person enjoy what they enjoy. Find a part worth taking part in. Look at an everyday activity and separate the pieces. For assembling a gift, someone could choose the item, select the paper, place it in a bag or decide which ribbon to use. For an outing, they could choose the destination or the music for the journey. Prepare the parts that would otherwise get in the way, using the support the person ordinarily has. Keep their chosen role meaningful. If they select the blue paper, use the blue paper. Their contribution should affect what happens. Before you begin Put the materials within comfortable reach and keep the workspace clear.Explain or show what is happening in a familiar way.Check whether the tools, closures and instructions are manageable with the usual assistance.Leave enough time for a response before adding another instruction.Make a pause or an early finish possible. A first try can be brief. Watching, choosing, doing one part or returning another day are all possible ways to join in. Offer assistance without making independence the price of participation, and let a refusal remain a refusal. Shop for access in the details. Before buying an activity or product, trace the steps between opening it and enjoying it. Does it require reading, precise timing, several tiny pieces or repeated setup? Can it be restarted easily? Is the enjoyable part accessible with the support already available? Clothes, accessories and everyday equipment Consider the wearer's preferred look alongside fabric, fit and fastenings. For a bag or device accessory, check actual dimensions, weight, access to controls and how it will be carried. A long feature list tells you very little about an awkward zip. Plans outside the house Ask about group size, noise, waiting, facilities and whether the usual support person can join. Find out what a shorter visit would involve and where a break can happen. A clear description or a few current photographs may help make the plan familiar. Keep personal information private when arranging support. Share the access details the host needs, and discuss photos separately rather than assuming participation includes being photographed. Afterward, consider what the teen seemed to enjoy and ask for their view in an accessible way. Keep the useful parts and adjust the awkward ones. A good activity leaves room for both help and personal choice.

title: Make room for the whole person.
summary: High support needs are part of everyday family life here. So are preferences, humor, privacy, favorite places and the pleasure of a day that works.
search: Profoundly AwesomeMake room for the whole person.High support needs are part of everyday family life here. So are preferences, humor, privacy, favorite places and the pleasure of a day that works.In this guideKeep the person in the conversation.Plan one good thing, with space around it.Let dignity shape the small decisions. Keep the person in the conversation. We use “profound autism” to describe our family's particular experience of very high support needs. The term is contested, and it is not everyone's preferred language. This is one family's perspective. Individual autistic people and families have their own experiences and ways of describing them. In everyday company, start by speaking to the person you are with. Make room for the communication methods they use and the time they need. Their usual support can be part of the conversation without the conversation passing them by. Ask about an actual preference, such as where to sit or what to do next.Keep familiar communication tools available and ask before touching them.Avoid piling several questions together or answering immediately on the person's behalf.Use a tone that respects their age, including when the words need to be straightforward. A person may need extensive help throughout the day. Their preferences still belong in the plan, including when they want to pause, decline or change direction.Read our detailed guide to multimodal communication, AAC, access methods and communication-partner support → Plan one good thing, with space around it. A swim, a familiar lunch, time outside or a favorite shop can be enough for a day out. Choose the part that matters most, then check the practical details that make it possible: arrival, waiting, food, bathrooms, breaks and the way home. Describe the plan in a familiar format. Actual photographs, objects, words or the person's established communication system may be useful. Include what comes afterward and how a change of plan will be explained. Keep a shorter version ready. Think through what happens if the visit is brief. Can you leave and return? Is there somewhere comfortable to pause? Can one family member finish an activity while another leaves with their support person? Agree on the practical arrangements before everyone is tired. Bring the everyday supplies and communication equipment the person ordinarily uses, and follow their existing support plans. Where possible, distribute the packing, transport and checking among the people available to help. Afterward, ask what worked and notice what the person chose to return to. Repeating a familiar pleasure is a perfectly good plan. A family day does not need a new destination every time. Let dignity shape the small decisions. Privacy matters at home, with friends and online. A difficult moment, personal care or an intimate detail can stay private. Before sharing a story or photograph, consider whose experience it is, what the person has communicated about it, and whether the detail needs to be public at all. Leave it out when permission is unclear. A useful handover can be brief. For an activity host or someone helping with the day, share the practical information they need: how the person communicates, what support helps them take part, how to offer a break and whom to contact if plans change. Keep private care information with the appropriate people through a suitable private channel. A simple starting point is: “Please speak directly to them and allow time to respond. They communicate using [method]. For this activity, [specific support] helps. If they want to pause, [familiar signal or arrangement].” Adapt it to the person and the setting. The useful questions remain ordinary ones. Did they have a say? Could they join in with the help they needed? Was there room to stop? Were their private moments protected? Those details make everyday life more considerate for the person at its center.

title: Build a quiet-break plan before you need it
summary: A break works better when nobody has to invent it in the middle of a crowded place. Decide where, how and what comes next while everyone is still calm.
search: Access · Days outBuild a quiet-break plan before you need itA break works better when nobody has to invent it in the middle of a crowded place. Decide where, how and what comes next while everyone is still calm. In this guideChoose the placeChoose the cuePlan the next stepRedefine success Find two possible pause points. Ask the venue where a lower-stimulation break can happen, then identify a second ordinary option such as the car, a bench outside or a quieter corner. A designated sensory room may be excellent, but it is not the only kind of pause that can help. Make the cue simple. Use the person’s familiar communication. The cue can be a word, symbol, gesture, photo or device button that means “break,” “outside,” “car,” “finished,” or another phrase they already use. Keep the communication method available rather than introducing a new system for the outing. Decide what happens after the break. A break does not have to mean the day is over, and returning does not have to be the goal. Before you go, choose a few valid options: return to the main activity, switch to the shorter version, get food, or go home. Keep the success measure human. Staying longer is not automatically better. Watching first, doing one part, taking several breaks or choosing to leave can all be successful participation. Build the plan around the person, not the admission price. Keep goingRelated guidesPlan the day outThe shorter-visit planAAC + communication

title: A New England rainy-day outing plan
summary: Rain does not have to cancel the day, but it does make transitions, wet clothes and backup food more important. Keep one main plan and one easy escape hatch.
search: Weekends · Weather-proofingA New England rainy-day outing planRain does not have to cancel the day, but it does make transitions, wet clothes and backup food more important. Keep one main plan and one easy escape hatch. In this guideOne anchorCar resetFood backupEasy exit Pick one indoor anchor. Choose the museum, pool, bookstore, café, aquarium or other indoor place that is worth leaving home for. Build the rest of the day around it rather than trying to fill every hour. Make the car part of the plan. Keep a dry layer, easy shoes, a bag for wet clothes and a towel where they can be reached without unpacking everything. On a wet day, the car can also be the simplest quiet-break space. Protect the food plan. Check kitchen hours and whether the place allows familiar food. Keep a backup that works for your family so the day does not depend on a café line or a menu that changed. Know the five-minute exit. Before entering, know how to get back to the car and what the short version of the outing looks like. A smaller day is still a day out. In this guideStart familiarLook closelyStyle mattersTest gently Copy the shape that already works. Note the cut, rise, sleeve length, waistband, collar and fabric of a favorite item before shopping. Comfort is often easier to reproduce when you identify the details rather than only the size on the label. Check the hidden irritants. Tags or printed labelsInner seams and bulky stitchingElastic strength and drawstringsZippers, snaps or buttonsFabric texture after washingHoods, cuffs and tight necklines Keep dressing age-respectful. Needing help with dressing does not make someone younger. Look for comfortable versions of the styles, colors and brands that suit their age and taste rather than defaulting to children’s designs. Buy one unknown at a time. When trying a new brand or fabric, start with one piece and keep the return deadline visible. Wash only after you know whether the item can be returned once washed. title: The shorter-visit plan
summary: Decide the small version of the outing before you arrive. It makes leaving a valid part of the plan instead of something that feels like the day went wrong.
search: Days out · A better exitThe shorter-visit planDecide the small version of the outing before you arrive. It makes leaving a valid part of the plan instead of something that feels like the day went wrong. In this guideThe anchorStopping pointsExit routeWhat counts Name the one thing you came for. Pick the swim, animal, exhibit, lunch or other part everyone is most interested in. If that happens, the day already has a center. Choose the natural stopping points. Examples include after one exhibit, after the pool, after lunch, or after the first thirty minutes. Natural stopping points make it easier to check whether everyone wants more. Make the exit ordinary. Know where the nearest exit is, how long it takes to reach the car, whether re-entry is possible, and what comes next. Keep the language matter-of-fact: “We’re finished here. Next is the car.” Do not grade the visit by duration. A twenty-minute visit can be exactly the right visit. The useful question is whether the person got to take part in a way that worked for them.
